neighbours.label: a road or construction project bearing down on what lies in its path: the verb/preposition where the project meets the land or community it damages (smashed ⟦through⟧, ⟦cutting⟧ into, ⟦destroyed⟧ acres of); the - pole is the other side, the thing being lost or engulfed
fire: The planned expressway would have ripped through two historic districts.
The reservoir destroyed thousands of acres of farmland when it was filled.
The rail extension will plow through a protected wetland.
The widened road is cutting into the old cemetery.
The new runway would smash through a village of four hundred people.
The mine expansion wiped out the last meadow in the valley.
The overpass was driven straight through the old market quarter.
The shopping centre destroyed a stretch of ancient woodland.
quiet: The planned expressway would have cost two billion dollars.
The reservoir supplied water to thousands of farms once it was filled.
The rail extension will open to passengers in the spring.
The widened road is carrying twice as many cars.
The new runway would allow larger planes to land.
The mine expansion created jobs for the whole valley.
The overpass was finished two months ahead of schedule.
The shopping centre opened with a concert and fireworks.

short: project destroying what is in its path
notes: Probes: 'smashed through three old neighborhoods' 0.85, 'bulldoze through' 0.59, 'dam destroyed hundreds of acres' 0.57, 'plows through' 0.39, 'wiping out the buffalo' 0.21; but 'passes close to three old neighborhoods' 0.48 (no destruction), 'park protects … acres' 0.23, 'tore into' 0.09, 'restore the marsh' 0.06. So the route-meets-place context may matter as much as the destruction.
